entries.title: How clouds form
entries.answer: A cloud is a group of very small water drops, ice crystals, or both. Air can carry water as an invisible gas called water vapor. When moist air rises and cools enough, some of the vapor can turn into tiny drops. They often form around very small specks floating in the air. At colder temperatures, ice crystals can form too. A cloud becomes visible because these drops and crystals scatter sunlight. Some clouds form right at ground level. We call those clouds fog.
facts: You can have a cloud without rain reaching the ground.

entries.title: How hurricanes get their strength
entries.answer: A hurricane is a large spinning storm that grows over warm ocean water. Warm, moist air rises from the sea. As it cools, water in the air forms clouds and gives off heat. That heat helps fuel more rising air and thunderstorms. The storm can pull in more moist air and keep growing. In a strong hurricane, the clouds may spin around a calmer center called the eye. A hurricane usually weakens after moving over land or much cooler water because it loses its supply of warm, moist ocean air.
facts: A hurricane has steady winds of at least 74 miles per hour.
Some regions call the same kind of storm a typhoon.

entries.title: How rainbows form
entries.answer: A rainbow can appear when sunlight shines into water drops in the air. The light bends on its way into a drop, bounces off the inside, and bends again as it leaves. The different colors bend by different amounts. Light reaching your eyes from some drops looks red, while light from drops at other angles looks blue or violet. Together these views make a colored arc. You can often find a rainbow by looking toward the rain when the Sun is behind you.
facts: A rainbow can be circular, although the ground often blocks the lower part from view.
A rainbow may appear in spray, even when it is not raining.

entries.title: The water cycle
entries.answer: The same water can be in the ocean one day and in a cloud another day. Some water at the ocean’s surface changes into a gas and mixes with the air. This is evaporation. As moist air cools, some of that gas turns back into tiny drops, forming clouds. When drops or ice crystals grow big enough, they can fall as rain or snow. Water may then soak into the ground, flow down a river, or stay frozen in ice for a long time. The water cycle follows all these paths, and has no single starting point.
facts: Sunlight supplies much of the energy for evaporation.
Some water that falls on land returns to the ocean in rivers.

quiz.explanation: Evaporation happens when some molecules escape from liquid water into the air as a gas.

entries.title: Weather and climate are different
entries.answer: Weather is what the air outside is like now or over a short stretch of time. It might be windy this morning and sunny this afternoon. Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years. If a place often has hot summers and little rain, those are parts of its climate. A cool or rainy day can still happen there. Scientists use records from many seasons and many years to work out what is common and whether those patterns are changing.
facts: Weather can change within a few minutes.
Scientists often use a 30-year period to describe a place’s usual weather.

entries.title: What a tornado is
entries.answer: A tornado is a fast-spinning column of air that reaches from a storm to the ground. Tornadoes sometimes grow from large thunderstorms that are already turning. Not all of those storms make tornadoes, and scientists are still working out why some do. You may see a funnel when tiny water drops form inside the spinning air. Dust and leaves can show where it touches down. A swirling funnel that stays above the ground is different from a tornado, even if the two look alike from far away.
facts: A tornado can touch the ground even if its visible funnel does not seem to reach all the way down.
A tornado is much smaller than a hurricane.

entries.title: What makes lightning and thunder
entries.answer: Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice can bump into each other and help separate electric charges. As the charges build up, electricity can suddenly move through the air. That flash is lightning. It can happen inside a cloud, between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. Lightning heats the air along its path very fast. The air swells outward, sending out a sound wave that we hear as thunder. We usually see the flash first because light reaches us much faster than sound.
facts: You can see distant lightning even when you cannot hear its thunder.
Lightning flashes can happen without touching the ground.
